content: 1. Are unique identifiers being utilized to eliminate duplicate case reporting (either at the point of diagnosis or during care) and to link information related to a single individual over time, across programs, and facilities? If so, which identifiers are being used, and how are they implemented? 2. In cases where multiple information systems and unique identifier systems are in use, do these systems have the capability to interoperate effectively? 3. What privacy, confidentiality, and data security laws, policies, and guidelines are currently in place? This includes regulations governing data collection, data standards, information access, data ownership, storage, transfer, use, disposal, and stewardship. What is the current status of their implementation and enforcement? 4. What physical and human resources are available to develop and operate electronic health information and medical record systems? Are there regional variations in resource availability across the country? 5. What is the availability of electricity, telephone, and internet connectivity at health facilities, district, subnational, and central levels? 6. What is the availability of computers, staff with computer skills, and facilities equipped with electronic medical or health records? 7. Have the unique identifier systems for health been evaluated for quality? If so, which systems were evaluated, when, by whom, and what were the results? Have recommendations from these evaluations been implemented to improve system quality? 8. Is information linked to uniquely identified health records being analyzed and used to track and improve the quality of: Individual prevention, diagnosis, care, and treatment at facility and program levels? Program overview and management at program, district, subnational, and country levels? 9. Are any identifiers being collected but not utilized? If so, what steps can be taken to incorporate them into case surveillance or patient monitoring systems? 10. Are names and dates of birth collected at HIV testing sites/services or HIV care/treatment sites? If names are not currently collected, is it feasible to do so in the future? How would patients and communities perceive the collection of identifiers among individuals diagnosed with HIV? 11. Have biometrics been used in the context of HIV? Have biometrics been used in any other settings? If so, provide details. 12. Are deaths routinely recorded in the country? Are death certificates required for burial? How are deaths recorded, and who is responsible for this process? Is there a death certificate, and what information does it include? If a cause of death is recorded, how is it determined? 13. Where and in what format are death records stored? What personal identifiers are included in these records? 14. Are there any health and demographic surveillance sites? Are death records available for linking with HIV case records? If so, have death records been successfully linked to HIV case records, and what was the outcome? 15. What are the resources and costs associated with operating current systems for case surveillance? What are the funding sources for surveillance, including electronic medical records (EMRs)? What is the potential for securing additional funding? 16. Can clinical facility staff report HIV cases? Do they have the time and motivation to do so? Is there someone within clinical settings who reports other infectious diseases, and can that system be expanded to include HIV case surveillance? How might this be achieved? 17. How can implementing partners assist in developing case surveillance? Which partners could be involved? 18. Are data security and patient privacy measures robust enough to support and instill confidence in an HIV case reporting system? 19. Does the Ministry of Health (MoH) have the capacity to receive and process electronic reports? Is there sufficient capacity for electronic reporting from sites and clinical laboratories? 20. What technological limitations within the country might impact case surveillance? What barriers are anticipated in developing case surveillance systems? 21. Can the evaluated system be expanded or adapted for national HIV case surveillance? What would this require, and what steps can be taken to advance the system? Are there elements that can be pilot-tested? 22. What are the resources and costs associated with operating the current patient monitoring system? What are the funding sources for patient monitoring, including electronic systems? What is the potential for securing additional funding? 23. Are facility staff able to adequately complete patient records, registers, and reports? Do they have the time and motivation to do so? How do districtor regional-level staff support patient monitoring, and how frequently? 24. How do districtor regional-level staff support joint reporting requirements by facilities, such as for TB/HIV or HIV/MNCH indicators? 25. How can implementing partners assist in improving patient monitoring? Which partners could be involved? 26. Are data security and patient privacy measures robust enough to support and instill confidence in an HIV patient monitoring system? 27. Does the Ministry of Health (MoH) have the capacity to receive and process electronic reports? Is there sufficient capacity for electronic reporting from sites and clinical laboratories? 28. What technological limitations within the country might impact patient monitoring? What barriers are anticipated in improving patient monitoring for both patient management and program monitoring? 29. Does the current patient monitoring system need to be adapted, expanded, or improved in line with new guidelines? What would this require, and what steps can be taken to advance the system? Are there elements that can be pilot-tested? 30. Is there anything else you would like to add? 31. Conduct a SWOT analysis of the results, identifying strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats. Based on this analysis, prioritize three to five high-priority elements for each SWOT category. 32. Develop a priority action plan scorecard summarizing the assessment findings, identifying priority costed improvement actions, and outlining support needs for implementation. Use this tool to monitor progress and evaluate the outcomes of interventions aimed at improving the HIV information system.
